# Key Takeaways

- Override a function by giving the derived class one with the same name, parameters, and `const`; a different parameter list hides the base version instead.
- Extend an override by calling the base version, `Person::print()`; without `Person::` the override calls itself forever.
- An override changes how a request is handled, never what the base promised.
- Two parents with a shared base give an object two copies of that base; prefer has-a to a diamond.

# Appendix

<!-- Slide 42 -->

## Overriding Functions: Good Practices

- Copy the base function's declaration exactly, then change only the body.
- Override only when the derived class must handle the same request differently.
- Keep every promise the base version makes.

<!-- Slide 43 -->

---

## Overriding Functions: Common Mistakes

- Changing the parameter list and hiding the base version instead of overriding it.
- Leaving off `const` and getting a second, separate function.
- Overriding a function so it does something the base version never did.

<!-- Slide 44 -->

---

## Overriding Functions: More Examples

~~~cpp
class Instructor : public Person {
private:
    string office;

public:
    Instructor(const string& n, int i, const string& o)
        : Person(n, i), office(o) { }

    void print() const {
        cout << getName() << " (" << getId() << "), office " << office << endl;
    }
};
~~~

- `ng.print()` shows the office; a Person or a Student still prints its own way.

## Calling Base Class Functions: Good Practices

- Extend the base version when the derived class adds to its behavior; replace it only when the behavior is truly different.
- Call the base version first unless the derived part must happen before it.
- Let the base class keep its own checks instead of copying them into the override.

<!-- Slide 49 -->

---

## Calling Base Class Functions: Common Mistakes

- Leaving off `Person::` and calling the override itself until the program crashes.
- Copying the base function's body into the override instead of calling it.
- Forgetting that the base version may already end the line.

<!-- Slide 50 -->

---

## Calling Base Class Functions: More Examples

~~~cpp
class GradStudent : public Student {
private:
    string advisor;

public:
    GradStudent(const string& n, int i, const string& m, const string& a)
        : Student(n, i, m), advisor(a) { }

    void print() const {
        Student::print();                           // which calls Person::print()
        cout << "Advisor: " << advisor << endl;
    }
};
~~~

- Each level calls the one directly above it. Outside a class, `raj.Person::print()` also works, but it is rarely needed.

## Multiple Inheritance and the Diamond Problem: Good Practices

- Use multiple inheritance only when both is-a sentences hold for everything each parent does.
- Write `public` in front of every parent.
- When two parents share a base, redesign with has-a before reaching for `virtual` inheritance.

<!-- Slide 55 -->

---

## Multiple Inheritance and the Diamond Problem: Common Mistakes

- Writing `public` only before the first parent.
- Calling a function both parents have and expecting the compiler to choose.
- Expecting the initializer list to change the order the parents are built.

<!-- Slide 56 -->

---

## Multiple Inheritance and the Diamond Problem: More Examples

~~~cpp
class Student : virtual public Person {
private:
    string major;

public:
    Student(const string& n, const string& m) : Person(n), major(m) { }
};

class TeachingAssistant : public Student, public Employee {
public:
    TeachingAssistant(const string& n, const string& m, double s)
        : Person(n), Student(n, m), Employee(n, s) { }
};
~~~

- With a virtual base, the most derived class builds it. Student's `Person(n)` runs only when a plain Student is built.
